newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan, Iraq agree to expand joint ventures.
newsitem.headline: Jordan, Iraq agree to expand joint ventures.

text.p: Jordan and Iraq agreed on Sunday to expand investments in agricultural and manufacturing projects undertaken by a jointly owned industrial holding company.

Jordan's Trade and Industry Minister Hani al-Mulqi and Iraqi Industry and Minerals Minister Adnan Abdul Majeed Jassim said at the end of an annual meeting of the state-owned Iraq-Jordan Industrial holding firm they had agreed to expand the firm's subsidiaries' projects, mostly in the agro-business.

"We are on the verge of expanding production capacity of this company and raising its products to international standards to allow for export markets in the future," Mulqi was quoted as saying by Jordan's state news agency Petra.
They also agreed to raise the capital of one of the subsidiaries which produces glucose to 3.5 million Jordanian dinars ($5 million) from 2.5 million dinars.

The Iraq-Jordan Industrial company was set up in 1987 with a capital of 20 million Iraqi dinars equally split between the two governments. It has mostly undertaken agricultural projects in Iraq, where a number of large-scale farms have been set up for dairy and meat production.
The company was concieved in the heyday of pan-Arab economic cooperation as part of ambitious plans to help integrate Jordanian and Iraqi industries.
"The prospects are extensive for expansion in industrial and agricultural projects between the two countries and the company aims to expand our industrial base," Jassim said.
The company's ambitious plans to set up industrial projects in both Iraq and Jordan were dealt a severe blow by U.N. sanctions on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Mulqi said he expected Jordanian industrialists to do better under Iraq's second phase of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations than the first phase, which secured exporters orders for humanitarian goods in excess of $140 million.

"There is a new opportunity now which Jordanian industrialists can benefit from after the first phase under which they gained experience in filling the forms and selling competitively priced goods," Mulqi said.
The oil-for-food deal, which allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months, went into effect last December and was renewed for another six months on June 8.
"Jordanian industry is capable of competing with its good quality goods and on prices and specifications," Mulqi added, saying Iraq was a main market for Jordanian products.
Baghdad will start buying the food once proceeds from the limited oil sales deal are placed in the U.N. escrow fund.

Jordanian industrialists have complained the U.N. sanction committee's delay in approving contracts won under the first deal eroded gains which initially put them second among countries awarded oil-for-food deals.
